# Mathematical Logic

Mathematical Logic is an important part of **Unit 1 – Discrete Structures and Optimization**.

The UGC NET syllabus includes:

- Propositional Logic
- Predicate Logic
- Propositional Equivalences
- Normal Forms
- Predicates and Quantifiers
- Nested Quantifiers
- Rules of Inference

---

## 1. Propositions

A **proposition** is a declarative statement that is either **True (T)** or **False (F)**, but not both.

### Examples

| Statement | Proposition? |
|---|---|
| 2 + 3 = 5 | Yes |
| Delhi is the capital of India. | Yes |
| 10 > 20 | Yes |
| What is your name? | No |
| Close the door. | No |

### Important Point

A proposition must have a definite truth value.

---

## 2. Logical Connectives

The basic logical connectives are:

| Symbol | Name |
|---|---|
| ¬p | NOT |
| p ∧ q | AND |
| p ∨ q | OR |
| p → q | Implication |
| p ↔ q | Biconditional |

---

## 3. NOT

The negation of `p` is written as:

$$
\neg p
$$

Truth table:

| p | ¬p |
|---|---|
| T | F |
| F | T |

---

## 4. AND

The conjunction of `p` and `q` is:

$$
p \land q
$$

It is **True only when both p and q are True**.

| p | q | p ∧ q |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | F |
| F | F | F |

### Remember

**AND → Both must be True.**

---

## 5. OR

The disjunction of `p` and `q` is:

$$
p \lor q
$$

It is False only when both propositions are False.

| p | q | p ∨ q |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | T |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | F |

### Remember

**OR → At least one must be True.**

---

## 6. Implication

Implication is written as:

$$
p \rightarrow q
$$

Read as:

> If p, then q.

Truth table:

| p | q | p → q |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | **F** |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | T |

### ⭐ UGC NET Important

An implication is **False only when:**

$$
p=T,\quad q=F
$$

Remember:

> **T → F = F**

All other cases are True.

---

## 7. Biconditional

Biconditional is written as:

$$
p \leftrightarrow q
$$

It is True when both propositions have the **same truth value**.

| p | q | p ↔ q |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | F |
| F | F | T |

---

# 8. Tautology

A proposition that is **always True** is called a tautology.

Example:

$$
p \lor \neg p
$$

Truth table:

| p | ¬p | p ∨ ¬p |
|---|---|---|
| T | F | T |
| F | T | T |

Therefore:

$$
p \lor \neg p
$$

is a **tautology**.

---

# 9. Contradiction

A proposition that is **always False** is called a contradiction.

Example:

$$
p \land \neg p
$$

| p | ¬p | p ∧ ¬p |
|---|---|---|
| T | F | F |
| F | T | F |

Therefore:

$$
p \land \neg p
$$

is a **contradiction**.

---

# 10. Contingency

A proposition that is **sometimes True and sometimes False** is called a contingency.

Example:

$$
p \land q
$$

Its truth value depends on the values of `p` and `q`.

---

# 11. Important Logical Equivalences

Some important equivalences for UGC NET are:

### Double Negation

$$
\neg(\neg p) \equiv p
$$

### De Morgan's Laws

$$
\neg(p \land q) \equiv \neg p \lor \neg q
$$

$$
\neg(p \lor q) \equiv \neg p \land \neg q
$$

### Implication

$$
p \rightarrow q \equiv \neg p \lor q
$$

### Biconditional

$$
p \leftrightarrow q
\equiv
(p \rightarrow q) \land (q \rightarrow p)
$$

---

# 12. Converse, Inverse and Contrapositive

For:

$$
p \rightarrow q
$$

### Converse

$$
q \rightarrow p
$$

### Inverse

$$
\neg p \rightarrow \neg q
$$

### Contrapositive

$$
\neg q \rightarrow \neg p
$$

### ⭐ Important

The original statement is logically equivalent to its contrapositive:

$$
p \rightarrow q
\equiv
\neg q \rightarrow \neg p
$$

But the converse is **not necessarily equivalent** to the original statement.

---

# 13. Normal Forms

Two important normal forms are:

### Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF)

CNF is an **AND of OR terms**.

Example:

$$
(p \lor q) \land (r \lor s)
$$

Structure:

**AND of ORs**

---

### Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF)

DNF is an **OR of AND terms**.

Example:

$$
(p \land q) \lor (r \land s)
$$

Structure:

**OR of ANDs**

---

# 14. Quick Memory Trick

### CNF

**C = Conjunction**

So:

**CNF → AND of ORs**

### DNF

**D = Disjunction**

So:

**DNF → OR of ANDs**

---

# 15. Practice Question

### Question 1

Which of the following is a tautology?

**A)** $p \land \neg p$

**B)** $p \lor \neg p$

**C)** $p \land q$

**D)** $p \rightarrow \neg p$

### Answer

**B) $p \lor \neg p$**

Because it is always True.

---

# 16. Practice Question

### Question 2

The implication:

$$
p \rightarrow q
$$

is false when:

**A)** p = T, q = T

**B)** p = T, q = F

**C)** p = F, q = T

**D)** p = F, q = F

### Answer

**B) p = T, q = F**

---

# 🎯 UGC NET Quick Revision

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| NOT | Reverses truth value |
| AND | Both True |
| OR | At least one True |
| Implication | False only for T → F |
| Biconditional | Same truth values |
| Tautology | Always True |
| Contradiction | Always False |
| CNF | AND of ORs |
| DNF | OR of ANDs |
| Contrapositive | ¬q → ¬p |
